comparison: Perfect agreement. Both evaluations support the genetic separation of pathogen susceptibility from lifespan pathways (C121-C123). OpenEval emphasizes this as an important result showing the two major phenotypes are genetically separable, while peer reviewers explicitly state the paper 'supports a model in which the increased lifespan and heightened pathogen susceptibility...result from the disruptions in the defecation motor program but through distinct pathways.'

Complete agreement. Both evaluations support the pathway independence from known CR components (C92-C96, C144). OpenEval notes the partial effect in aak-2 mutants suggesting some interaction, while peer reviewers accept the comprehensive genetic analysis as demonstrating 'robust results' using 'classic epistasis analyses' to distinguish pathway relationships.

Strong agreement. Both support the comparison between regular-but-slow DMP (clk-1, isp-1) versus disrupted DMP (flr-1, nhx-2, pbo-1) as providing mechanistic insight (C70-C75). OpenEval emphasizes this distinguishes different types of DMP alterations, while peer reviewers note this 'further reinforces the proposed model' linking DMP defects to both phenotypes.

Full agreement. Both evaluations support HLH-30 requirement for lifespan extension (C8, C98-C100, C103-C104). OpenEval notes the slight lifespan increase with nhx-2 knockdown suggests some complexity, while peer reviewers accept that 'the lifespan extension is dependent on hlh-30' and treat the genetic epistasis data as demonstrating HLH-30's necessity.

Complete agreement. Both support the calorie restriction mimicry claim (C7, C80, C82, C84, C87-C89). OpenEval emphasizes multiple molecular markers and genetic epistasis with eat-2, noting the lack of additivity provides strong evidence for pathway overlap. Peer reviewers explicitly accept that 'defective defecation motor program leads to intestine bloating and compromised nutrient absorption' resulting in calorie restriction effects.

Strong agreement on DMP defects and their consequences. OpenEval R1 addresses comprehensive DMP characterization (C54-C69, C77-C78) with multiple genetic approaches and functional assays. Peer R2 explicitly accepts the mechanistic finding, stating 'the authors show that disruption of tax-6 decreases the rate of defecation leading to intestinal accumulation of bacteria.' Both treat the DMP defect data as robust and convincing, though they emphasize slightly different aspects of the evidence.

Strong agreement on dual phenotype. OpenEval R2 addresses increased pathogen susceptibility with multiple genetic approaches and epistasis analysis (C29-C32, C40, C42-C49). Peer R1 explicitly acknowledges the dual phenotype as a core finding with 'convincing evidence,' stating the study shows 'disruption of calcineurin...results in increased susceptibility to P. aeruginosa but extends lifespan.' Both evaluations support the pathogen susceptibility claims, though OpenEval provides more detailed analysis of the epistasis data.

Complete agreement. Both support NHR-8 requirement and upregulation (C9-C10, C107, C117-C120). OpenEval emphasizes the genetic demonstration, transcriptional upregulation, and epistasis with daf-9, while peer reviewers accept that 'nhr-8, whose levels are increased by deficits in defecation' is 'necessary for the increased lifespan.' Both treat NHR-8 as a supported downstream effector.

Agreement on pathway independence from canonical immunity. OpenEval R2 addresses epistasis with immunity pathway mutants (C43-C49), noting the more pronounced effect in pmk-1 mutants suggests some interaction. Peer R6 accepts this independence, noting 'classic epistasis analyses were used to distinguish between genes operating in the same or separate pathways' with 'robust results.' Both support the claim that the pathogen susceptibility mechanism is independent of canonical immunity pathways.

Agreement with different emphasis. OpenEval R10 addresses differential effects of tax-6 versus crh-1/crtc-1 on pathogen susceptibility (C36-C37), noting this is based on a single comparative experiment. Peer R6 accepts pathway independence from canonical immunity more broadly (C36-C37, C43-C49), treating the epistasis analyses as robust evidence. Both support the independence claims, though peer review encompasses broader evidence.

Agreement on enhanced colonization. OpenEval R3 addresses enhanced bacterial colonization using imaging and CFU assays (C50-C52), providing a mechanistic link between DMP defects and pathogen susceptibility. Peer R2 accepts this as part of the broader mechanistic finding about DMP disruption leading to intestinal accumulation of bacteria. Both treat the colonization data as supporting evidence.

Agreement on lifespan extension. OpenEval R9 addresses lifespan extension with multiple genetic approaches and fer-1 control (C33, C41), noting this is confirmatory of prior work. Peer R1 accepts this as part of the dual phenotype core finding. Both support the lifespan extension claims, though peer review integrates this into the broader dual phenotype narrative.

Agreement on NHR-8/DAF-9 epistasis. OpenEval R6 includes epistasis with daf-9 (C109-C110) as part of comprehensive NHR-8 pathway analysis. Peer R10 accepts this finding as part of the mechanistic dissection, implicitly validating it within the praised comprehensive genetic analysis. Both support this epistatic relationship.

Agreement on technical controls. OpenEval R5 includes RNAi efficiency controls (C102) as supporting the HLH-30 findings. Peer R11 does not raise concerns about technical controls (C102 among others), implicitly accepting them. Both evaluations validate these control experiments.

Partial overlap on core claims. OpenEval R1 extensively addresses DMP characterization (C3-C4 among many others), while Peer R1 addresses the dual phenotype broadly (C3-C4 among others). Both include C3-C4 but focus on different aspects: OpenEval on detailed DMP phenotypic characterization, peer review on the overall dual phenotype finding.

Minimal overlap. OpenEval R3 addresses enhanced colonization mechanistically (C5, C50-C52), while Peer R1 addresses the broad dual phenotype (C5 among others). Both include C5 but in very different contexts: OpenEval focuses on colonization assays, peer review on the overall finding of pathogen susceptibility and lifespan extension.

Minimal overlap on technical controls. OpenEval R4 includes RNAi efficiency control in eat-2 mutants (C86) as addressing a technical concern for CR mimicry claims. Peer R11 accepts technical controls broadly (C86 among others) without specific challenge. Both validate this control experiment.

Minimal overlap on technical controls. OpenEval R6 includes RNAi efficiency controls (C112) for NHR-8 pathway analysis. Peer R11 accepts technical controls broadly (C112 among others) as implicitly validated. Both support these control experiments.

Minimal overlap on technical controls. OpenEval R1 includes multiple genetic approaches and controls (C55 among many others) for DMP characterization. Peer R11 accepts technical controls broadly (C55 among others) without raising concerns. Both validate these control experiments.

Peer review only. Peer R12 addresses established background facts from literature (C1-C2, C21, C25-C26, C28) that reviewers treat as accepted context. OpenEval does not have a corresponding result evaluating these background/literature claims, as OpenEval results focus on novel experimental findings rather than literature context.
